$comment: DRAFT — variation layer. Art direction only. It never restates a dimension;
it says how much of the standard's legal range to exploit, and how far past
it to let things drift.
This is the half that changes constantly. The standards layer is verified
once against a manual; this gets art-directed every time a look changes,
which is exactly why they are separate files.
Every entry REFERENCES a parameter in a typology. It cannot introduce one.
A reference to a parameter that no longer exists must fail loudly at load —
silent fallback is how a 'weathered' profile quietly stops weathering.
The point of separating in_spec from out_of_spec: a sign that is merely at
the low end of its legal mounting height is CORRECT, just short. A sign 4 cm
below the legal minimum is NEGLECTED. Those read completely differently and
an artist needs to dial them independently.
label: Weathered urban
description: A street that has been maintained, then not maintained for about fifteen years. Nothing is broken; everything has drifted.

seed.note: Read per instance so two signs on the same pole differ, and so a scene is reproducible. Falls back to the tool's own seed parm when absent.

$comment: uniform     — flat across the range. Honest default when nothing is known.
normal      — clusters at nominal. Right for things a crew tried to get right.
skew_low    — clusters low. Right for settling, sagging, sinking.
bimodal     — two clusters. Right for 'replaced recently' vs 'original'.

in_spec.$comment: Crews aim for nominal and miss downward; nothing gets installed too high by accident.

out_of_spec.$comment: Posts settle into soft ground. Below-minimum is a real and common defect.
Knocked by a vehicle or a plough, never straightened. The single most legible sign of neglect, and cheap to produce.

in_spec.$comment: Bimodal, not uniform: posts get replaced individually over decades, so a street carries two or three vintages side by side. This is the parameter that most rewards not being uniform.

$comment: Correlations are declared in the STANDARDS layer because they are
engineering, not taste. This layer only says whether to honour them.
Breaking one is itself a look: a replacement post on an original footing
is a real thing you see. But it must be deliberate and rare, never the
accidental result of jittering every parameter independently — that is
precisely what makes procedural work read as procedural.
Hooks for the Copernicus aging work rather than geometry. Age drives the
masks; the retroreflective response degrades long before a sign looks
obviously old, which is why sheeting_retroreflectivity is separate from
the visible dirt.
Fade is channel-dependent: reds and oranges go first, which is why old
signs go pink. A single fade scalar gets this wrong.
